I am also curious about the genetic profile of the ancient Macedonians. I am not entirely convinced that the samples we currently have are representative of the ancient Macedonian population as a whole.

To the west, we have the Illyrians, who appear to have had relatively high levels of Steppe ancestry and lower levels of Anatolian Neolithic Farmer (ANF) ancestry. To the east, we have the Thracians, whose genetic profiles seem somewhat closer to those of the Mycenaeans, with relatively higher ANF ancestry and lower Steppe ancestry than the Illyrians. Interestingly, many Thracian samples also seem to be associated with haplogroup E-V13. How the Thracians came to speak an Indo-European language despite these apparent genetic differences remains an intriguing question.

The Logkas samples, on the other hand, may represent an early population related to the Proto-Greco-Phrygian linguistic community. However, in my opinion, these samples cannot necessarily be considered representative of any particular population, especially given their high levels of Yamnaya-related Steppe ancestry. Their chronology is also relatively early, which makes it difficult to extrapolate their genetic profile to later populations.

Furthermore, the geographical boundaries of ancient Macedonia did not necessarily correspond to those of the modern Greek region of Macedonia or the present-day state of North Macedonia. The region was inhabited by various populations, including Illyrian- and Brygian-related groups in the west, as well as Thracian and Mygdonian groups in the east. Farther north, the Paeonians occupied an area where Illyrian and Thracian influences may have overlapped.

If the traditions and legends concerning the origins of the Macedonian royal dynasty and people preserve some historical memory of a migration from southern Greece, perhaps from Thessaly or even the Peloponnese, this raises another question: to what extent did the historical Macedonians originate outside the region they eventually inhabited? Such traditions should, of course, be treated cautiously rather than taken as straightforward historical evidence.

The presence of Y-DNA haplogroup J2a in one of the samples is also noteworthy. It could reflect connections with the Mycenaean world, the presence of J2a lineages within the ancient Macedonian population itself, or a possible connection with populations from the Thracian sphere. However, a single Y-DNA lineage cannot establish the overall ancestry or ethnic identity of an individual or population.

Ultimately, I think we need more geographically diverse and chronologically representative ancient DNA samples before drawing firm conclusions about the genetic profile of the ancient Macedonians and their relationship to neighbouring populations, including the Illyrians, Thracians, and Mycenaeans.
